import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

## The setup

A common pattern in this codebase: a design memo is `status: draft` ("draft for review") with concrete type signatures + a service interface, but the implementation is gated on user acceptance. Examples:

- The `dogfood-design-memo-binding-service-api-2026-05-24` memo specifies `BindingRecord`, a 5-operation `BindingService` interface, and a 9-variant `BindingServiceError` union. The implementation (Phase 1b P-068) waits on the user's review.
- The `dogfood-design-memo-device-attestation-ux-2026-05-24` memo specifies a 3-screen modal flow. The UI implementation waits on the same review.

You're sitting on hours of safe overnight work and the memo is ready enough to type-check. What do you ship?

## The pattern

**Split: types now, behavior on memo-acceptance.**

Extract just the type declarations — `BindingRecord`, the error union, the permission enum, pure helpers like `composeBindingId` / `parseBindingId` / `hasRequiredPermission` — into a `*-types.ts` module. No service implementation, no I/O, no behavior the user would object to.

Example from this codebase: `packages/operator-core/lib/harness/binding-types.ts` (commit `f05997aa`). 120 LOC + 15 unit tests, all pure functions. The eventual `binding-service.ts` (when the memo is accepted) will `import` from here verbatim.

## Why it works

Three reasons.

**(1) Types-only is reversible.** If the memo revises (e.g. adds a column to `BindingRecord`, swaps the error code shape), the types-only file changes alongside. Every downstream consumer gets a typecheck error to update. No runtime to break, no DB schema to migrate, no API to deprecate. It's the lightest possible commitment to a design.

**(2) The implementing agent gets a head start.** When the memo lands as accepted, P-068's first commit doesn't have to define the types — they already exist, already pass lint, already have unit tests. The implementer reads "the service surface is `BindingService` from binding-types.ts" and starts wiring methods. Days saved.

**(3) The user reviewing the memo can see types in tree.** "Does the `BindingRecord` shape make sense?" → the user can navigate to the file, scroll through the comments, see how `composeBindingId` encodes things, run the tests. Reviewing a memo with a real types file open is qualitatively different from reviewing a memo with no code at all. The review becomes "is the implementation I see in tree what I want?" — a more concrete question than "is the design as written what I want?"

## What NOT to do

Don't ship anything that requires user judgment:

| Safe to ship | Wait for memo acceptance |
|---|---|
| Type declarations | Service implementations |
| Pure functions (parsers, predicates, encoders) | Functions that perform I/O |
| Error union variants | Error-handling policies (retry counts, backoff) |
| Constant tables (e.g. required permissions) | Wiring those tables into UI behavior |
| Tests for the pure functions | Tests that assert behavior the memo hasn't pinned |
| New SQL columns (additive only) | New SQL tables that imply a new domain |

The line is: *would the user reading the diff say "that's what I'd have written"?* If yes, ship. If they'd say "wait, that's a decision," wait.

<Aside type="tip">
The commit message matters. State clearly: "types-only — implementation gated on memo acceptance." Reviewers should know this is groundwork, not a service launch. Use phrasing that signals reversibility: "If you revise the memo, the types change; downstream consumers get typecheck errors to update."
</Aside>

## What this is NOT

This is not the same as [`forward-defined-registry-entries`](/internal/docs/agent-insights/forward-defined-registry-entries/) — that pattern is about *registering* something ahead of its full implementation (e.g., a query name mapped before the resolver exists). Types-first is about *publishing the type surface* of an unimplemented service so the eventual implementation has a stable spine.

Both patterns are about decoupling "the user has accepted this" from "the next coder can start." Different mechanisms, same shape.

## The risk: types that get stale

If the memo never lands (user rejects, scope changes, plan deprecates), the types-only module becomes dead code. Two mitigations:

1. **Cross-link the memo from the types file.** The header comment should name the memo slug. If the memo is deleted, a future cleanup pass greps the types file's references and removes the orphan.
2. **Be honest in the commit message about the dependency.** "Per plan-store entry `dogfood-design-memo-binding-service-api-2026-05-24` (still 'draft for review')." Anyone reading `git log` knows the type spine is provisional.
